newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin proposes telephone hotline with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin proposes telephone hotline with Japan.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Friday proposed a telephone hotline between Moscow and Tokyo, saying he was disappointed by relations between the two countries.
"I propose that contacts should take various shapes, including by telephone," Yeltsin said at the start of a breakfast meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
"Your Chancellery and the Kremlin must have a direct line." He added: "I am disappointed by the level of relations."
Yeltsin, attending his fifth summit of the Group of Seven leading industrialised states, arrived in Denver on Thursday to press his case for full Russian membership of the rich countries' club.
The Russian leader will attend almost all the sessions of the three-day "mile-high" summit.

But Hashimoto told reporters before he arrived that he hoped the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- would continue to exclude Russia from summit talks on financial and macro-economic issues.

Japanese officials in Denver have, however, highlighted improving relations between the two countries and some said on Thursday they expected Hashimoto to take up an offer from Yeltsin to hold annual summits.
Hashimoto said as he arrived for the start of the breakfast meeting that it was "hard to predict" whether he would visit Russia soon.

Russia hopes for Japanese investment to help develop its natural resources, especially in the energy-rich Pacific region, but ties between the two states have been strained for decades due to a dispute about the ownership of four islands seized by the Soviet army in the final days of World War Two.

Japan says that the islands, which it terms the Northern Territories, must be returned. Yeltsin, aware that any territorial concessions would prompt a fierce backlash from his nationalist opponents, says there is no question of that.
The dispute has prevented the two states signing a formal treaty ending World War Two hostilities.
"The president told the premier that former Soviet missiles are still targeted at Japan, and that the time has come to take Japan off the targets," the official said.

He said that Yeltsin had stressed the need for regular summit meetings between the two leaders, although Hashimoto's schedule was so tight that a meeting might have to take place on a weekend in the Russian Far East.

"Yeltsin said it was important for the two leaders to visit each other on occasions other than international conferences," the spokesman said, adding that the leaders had also accepted the idea of a new initiative to boost Japanese investment.

Ties between Russia and Japan have been frosty for decades because of a dispute over ownership of four islands seized by Soviet troops in the closing days of the Second World War. Japan wants the islands back. Yeltsin, fearing opposition from nationalists, rules this idea out.
